analysis.one_liner: Makes war profiteering and fraud in Iraq reconstruction a federal crime with 20-year prison terms and profit forfeiture.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made it a crime to deliberately overcharge on Iraq war and reconstruction contracts, never got a vote — it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Iraq war, the U.S. was paying private companies billions to rebuild the country and supply the military. This bill would have made it a federal crime to defraud the government or deliberately overvalue goods and services connected to the Iraq war or reconstruction, punishable by up to 20 years in prison and fines of $1 million or double the profits. It also would have let the government seize profits from such fraud and treat the money as criminal proceeds under money-laundering laws.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers, who funded the Iraq war and reconstruction through their tax dollars and would benefit if inflated billing and fraudulent contracts were deterred, and American troops, who depended on contractors for supplies and services.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to run a scheme to defraud the U.S. or Iraq, make false statements, or materially overvalue goods or services with the intent to profit excessively from Iraq war or reconstruction work, punishable by up to 20 years in prison [S3].
Sets fines at the greater of $1 million or twice the gross profits from the offense, so penalties scale with what a contractor took [S3].

Adds the offense to civil and criminal forfeiture laws, letting the government seize money and property traceable to war profiteering, and brings such transactions under federal money-laundering statutes [S3].
Applies extraterritorial jurisdiction and flexible venue, so prosecutions are not blocked by the fact that the conduct happened in Iraq [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Government contractors doing Iraq war and reconstruction work: honest ones would face a new layer of legal exposure, and fraudulent ones would face prison, profit-stripping fines, and forfeiture of proceeds.

drawbacks.text: The key offense turns on whether someone 'materially overvalued' a good or service 'with the specific intent to excessively profit' — a vague standard that could reach routine pricing judgments and contract disputes, not just clear-cut fraud [S3].
Federal fraud and false-claims laws already criminalize cheating the government on contracts, so the bill adds mainly stiffer war-specific penalties rather than closing a gap in the law [S3].
The law was written to expire once major combat ended, Iraq got its own government, and a State Department-led U.S. mission took over assistance — limiting how long the deterrence would last [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: wartime reconstruction involved tens of billions in taxpayer money flowing to contractors with weak oversight, and a dedicated crime with profit forfeiture would raise the price of cheating. The cost is that the 'excessive profit' standard is imprecise and could create legal risk for contractors making good-faith pricing calls in chaotic conditions; honest supporters would have to acknowledge that vagueness. On balance it targeted a documented taxpayer risk, but its drafting was blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its crime subcommittee in January 2004, and never moved again — no markup, no floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rahm Emanuel introduced the bill on December 8, 2003, with 16 original cosponsors including progressives and moderates [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].
On January 15, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill finished the 108th Congress with no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors doing Iraq war and reconstruction work are better off, because no new criminal penalty or profit forfeiture ever applied to overcharging or fraud on those contracts.

for.name: Rahm Emanuel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the War Profiteering Prevention Act of 2003 in the House.

for.name: 56 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 57 total cosponsors including one Independent.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and majority of the House Judiciary Committee (R-led)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill sat in the crime subcommittee from January 15, 2004 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders — no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never advanced it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have exposed contractors who overcharged or defrauded on Iraq work to 20-year prison terms, fines of up to double their profits, and forfeiture of proceeds. By dying without a vote, it left existing fraud law as the only check on billing practices during the multibillion-dollar reconstruction.

The crime was limited to Iraq-related work and was written to expire once the occupation ended and a State Department-led mission took over, limiting the exposure for contractors with long-term government business.
